content: Induction of labor refers to the artificial stimulation of uterine contractions to initiate the process of childbirth. Various methods, including pharmacological, surgical, and mechanical techniques, are employed for this purpose. Membrane sweeping is a mechanical method in which a healthcare provider inserts one or two fingers into the cervix and performs a circular sweeping motion to separate the lower part of the amniotic sac (membranes) from the uterine wall. This action is thought to release hormones that promote cervical effacement and dilation, potentially leading to the onset of labor. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects and safety of membrane sweeping for inducing labor in women who are at or near term (36 weeks of gestation or later). The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing membrane sweeping with placebo, no treatment, or other labor induction methods. A total of 44 studies involving 6,940 women and their infants were analyzed. The certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach, and the overall risk of bias in the studies was considered low or unclear. When comparing membrane sweeping to no treatment or a sham procedure (40 studies, 6,548 participants), the following findings were observed: Women who underwent membrane sweeping were more likely to experience spontaneous onset of labor (average risk ratio [aRR] 1.21, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.08 to 1.34, based on low-certainty evidence). These women were less likely to require formal induction of labor (aRR 0.73, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.94, based on low-certainty evidence). There was little to no difference between groups in the rates of cesarean delivery (aRR 0.94, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.04, moderate-certainty evidence), spontaneous vaginal birth (aRR 1.03, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.07, moderate-certainty evidence), maternal death or serious morbidity (aRR 0.83, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.20, low-certainty evidence), or neonatal death or serious morbidity (aRR 0.83, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.17, low-certainty evidence). When membrane sweeping was compared to vaginal or intracervical prostaglandins (4 studies, 480 participants), the following results were noted: There was little to no difference in the likelihood of spontaneous onset of labor (aRR 1.24, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.57, low-certainty evidence), induction of labor (aRR 0.90, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.45, low-certainty evidence), cesarean delivery (aRR 0.69, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.09, low-certainty evidence), spontaneous vaginal birth (aRR 1.12, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.32, low-certainty evidence), maternal death or serious morbidity (aRR 0.93, 95% CI 0.27 to 3.21, low-certainty evidence), or neonatal death or serious morbidity (aRR 0.40, 95% CI 0.12 to 1.33, low-certainty evidence). When membrane sweeping was compared to intravenous oxytocin with or without amniotomy (1 study, 104 participants), the findings were as follows: There was little to no difference in the rates of spontaneous onset of labor (aRR 1.32, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.96, low-certainty evidence), induction of labor (aRR 0.51, 95% CI 0.05 to 5.42, low-certainty evidence), or cesarean delivery (aRR 0.69, 95% CI 0.12 to 3.85, low-certainty evidence). Maternal death or serious morbidity was reported, but no events occurred in the study. When membrane sweeping was compared to vaginal or oral misoprostol (2 studies, 160 participants), there was little to no difference in the rate of cesarean delivery (risk ratio [RR] 0.82, 95% CI 0.31 to 2.17, low-certainty evidence). One study (355 participants) compared once-weekly membrane sweeping with twice-weekly membrane sweeping and a sham procedure. The results showed little to no difference in the rates of induction of labor (RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.85, low-certainty evidence), cesarean delivery (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.46, low-certainty evidence), spontaneous vaginal birth (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.17, moderate-certainty evidence), maternal death or serious morbidity (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.30 to 2.02, low-certainty evidence), or neonatal death or serious morbidity (RR 2.00, 95% CI 0.18 to 21.76, low-certainty evidence). No studies were identified that compared membrane sweeping with amniotomy alone or other mechanical methods of labor induction. Three studies (675 participants) reported that women generally had a favorable experience with membrane sweeping. In one study, 88% of women surveyed postpartum indicated that they would choose membrane sweeping in a future pregnancy. Two studies (290 participants) suggested that membrane sweeping may be more cost-effective than prostaglandins, but further research is needed in this area. In conclusion, membrane sweeping may be effective in promoting the spontaneous onset of labor, but the certainty of the evidence supporting this is low. Compared to expectant management, membrane sweeping may reduce the need for formal labor induction. However, questions remain regarding the optimal frequency, timing, and gestational age for performing membrane sweeping to achieve the best outcomes.
